title: What is known about 1RB1LF_1RC1RF_0LD1RE_---1LC_0RB1RE_1LA0LE
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LF_1RC1RF_0LD1RE_---1LC_0RB1RE_1LA0LE.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape. Its right end is a pool of 1s that pays for a doubling block of pairs. The complete map from one right-end visit to the next is now known: for an even pool it is a doubling map, u ↦ 2u modulo m, whose modulus m grows by one at every doubling that does not wrap. The machine can halt only when a doubling lands exactly on m at one of the special moduli 2<sup>k+1</sup> − k.
verdict: The question is open. At every right-end visit in state B the tape is T(c, a, b) = [1^2 0 (10)^c] 1^a 0 (10)^b B>0. With an even pool a, and u = b + 2, m = a/2 + b + 3, the next visit is T(c, a − 2b − 2, 2b + 2) when 2u < m (u doubles, m grows by one); when 2u > m a carry replaces u by 2u − m; when 2u = m the pool becomes odd: T(c, 2m − 3, 0). An odd pool is doubled down until it cannot pay, then leaves a bracket behind or swallows the one that is there. The only halting visits are T(none, 1, b), reached exactly from odd pools A = 2k+2 − 2k − 3 without a bracket. The machine halts iff this right-end map reaches T(none, 1, b): a theorem checked by Lean's kernel.

How far it has been followed. The exact map (c/fast.c) was run for 1011 operations: 50,000,005,600 right-end visits, of the order of 1031 machine steps, 35 odd pools, 18 of them without a bracket, none of them a halting one (the closest: 989 against 1005). A later halt needs an exact hit at a modulus beyond 237; heuristically that has probability about 10−11. Halting configurations of the same form exist (T(none, 12, 19) halts after five visits), so there is no parity or congruence argument; the map is a chaotic doubling map and no proof is in sight.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (D0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 2,930 cells have been visited and 1,686 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: It halts iff the right-end map reaches T(none, 1, b)
claims.text: The map F on nodes (the visits T(c, a, b), and the fresh sweep that a pool of one starts at w = 1) is proved move by move on the tape: rounds, the end of a sweep, carries, the even and odd events, the bracket an odd pool leaves behind, the merge of a pool of three into the bracket, each with its short cases. Then: the machine halts from blank tape iff the orbit of T(none, 2, 0) (step 7) under F reaches a visit T(none, 1, b). Evaluated: the first 100 nodes (kernel) and 104 (native_decide) do not halt.

claims.title: The building blocks of the map, for all parameters
claims.text: Each move of the map between two visits is a Lean theorem about every value of its counts and every tape in its context: the start of a sweep, a round (two 1s of the pool and one pair of the tail become four 1s of the middle block), the end of a sweep (the middle block becomes the doubled pair block), the carry (the middle block becomes the pool), the two events where pool and tail run out together (one makes the pool odd), the birth of a bracket and its merge. They are not yet assembled into one statement of the whole map. Fifteen more rules in the forms the assembly uses (pools of one, two and three, the short tails, the bracket and merge cases) are generated the same way.

claims.title: T(none, 1, n) halts for every n
claims.text: From 0^∞ 1 0 (10)^n B> 0^∞ the machine reaches state D on a 0, the undefined transition, after 2n + 6 steps.

claims.title: The complete right-end map
claims.text: step(c, a, b) gives the next visit for every T(c, a, b): rounds, doubling, carry, odd-pool events, bracket birth and merge, and the few double coincidences. It agrees with direct simulation on 13,728 configurations (c none or 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 10; a < 40; b < 44), on every visit of the first 3·106 steps of the run, and on all 2,066 visits of the first 3·109 steps.

claims.title: Even pools: doubling modulo a growing modulus
claims.text: For even a, with u = b + 2 and m = a/2 + b + 3: 2u < m gives a visit with (2u, m + 1); 2u > m is a carry to (2u − m, m); 2u = m gives T(c, 2m − 3, 0). Checked against step for 7,080 configurations.

claims.title: Which odd pools halt
claims.text: An odd pool without bracket always starts at T(none, A, 0), and the doubling steps bring it to exactly 1 iff A = 2k+2 − 2k − 3 (1, 3, 9, 23, 53, 115, …), which for a pool born at 2u = m (A = 2m − 3) means m = 2k+1 − k. (A merge that ends exactly as the tail runs out can also leave an odd pool without bracket, T(none, 2c + p + 9, 0); the model covers it.) Checked against step for all odd A < 400.

claims.title: No halt in 10<sup>11</sup> operations of the map
claims.text: The map in C (the same first 20,000 visits as the Python model) runs 10<sup>11</sup> operations, 50,000,005,600 visits, without a halt; a/2 + b reaches 5.0·10<sup>10</sup>, of the order of 10<sup>31</sup> machine steps by the growth law steps ≈ (a/2 + b)<sup>3</sup>/3 (the step count itself is not computed). 35 odd pools appear, 18 without bracket: 5, 13, 165, 989, 1853, 13309, 26333, 44669, 49909, 19855861, 169438117, 283866789, 1487681501, 1992437437, 3603147421, 10918121213, 46694013501, 51055443101; all are 5 mod 8.

claims.title: A later halt is very unlikely
claims.text: The map spends about two operations at each modulus m and each hits 2u = m with chance about 1/m, so the target m = 2<sup>k+1</sup> − k is hit with chance about 2<sup>−k</sup>; the targets still ahead start at k = 36, about 10<sup>−11</sup> in total. The modulus is not monotone (merges and new brackets move it), so this is an estimate.

claims.title: Why no congruence helps
claims.text: With D = m − u, an event at modulus m needs D = m/2<sup>i</sup> on arrival with 2<sup>i</sup> dividing m, so every event after the first has 4 | m, and a target m = 2<sup>k+1</sup> − k needs i ≤ v<sub>2</sub>(k). Backwards a state (D, m) has two predecessors, one or none according to the parities of D and m, one on average: a critical branching process, so the states that reach a target thin out like 1/m without any residue class being excluded.

claims.title: Does an event ever fall on a target modulus?
claims.text: Halting configurations of the form T exist and are reachable by the map (T(none, 12, 19) halts), and events with m ≡ 0 mod 4 leave one target in four possible, so no congruence excludes a halt. Deciding the machine means deciding a chaotic doubling map with a moving modulus.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows whether it halts. A pool of 1s pays for a block of pairs that doubles at every sweep; in numbers, the machine doubles a counter u modulo a slowly growing modulus m. It can halt only if a doubling lands exactly on m at one of the rare moduli 2^(k+1) − k.

facts.text: The map for even pools; m grows by one at each doubling that does not wrap.
Of the exact map without a halt: 5·10<sup>10</sup> visits, about 10<sup>31</sup> steps.
The building blocks of the map and the halting visit, proved in Lean for all parameters.

sections.heading: A pool, a block of pairs, and a doubling map
html: Each time the head pushes the tape one cell further right (in state B), the tape is a pool of a 1s, a 0, and a block of b pairs 10: 1^a 0 (10)^b. Sometimes a bracket 1^2 0 (10)^c sits to the left of the pool.

Doubling. One sweep turns the block of b pairs into 2b + 2 pairs and takes 2b + 2 ones from the pool. Inside the sweep the machine works in rounds: each round moves two 1s out of the pool and one pair out of the old block, and adds four 1s to a middle block that becomes the new pair block at the end.

Carry. If the pool runs dry in the middle of a sweep, the middle block becomes the new pool and the sweep goes on with what is left of the old block. In numbers: put u = b + 2 and m = a/2 + b + 3. A sweep without carry doubles u and adds one to m. A carry replaces u by 2u − m. So the machine computes u ↦ 2u modulo m, over and over, with a modulus that creeps up by one each time the doubling does not wrap around.

<svg viewBox="0 0 560 118" role="img" aria-label="The doubling map" style="max-width:560px;width:100%;height:auto;font:13px sans-serif"><rect x="8" y="12" width="150" height="40" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/><text x="83" y="37" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">2u < m: double</text><rect x="205" y="12" width="150" height="40" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/><text x="280" y="37" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">2u > m: carry</text><rect x="402" y="12" width="150" height="40" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="477" y="37" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">2u = m: odd pool</text><text x="83" y="76" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">u → 2u, m → m + 1</text><text x="280" y="76" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">u → 2u − m</text><text x="477" y="76" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">pool = 2m − 3</text><text x="83" y="100" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" opacity=".7">almost always</text><text x="280" y="100" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" opacity=".7">almost always</text><text x="477" y="100" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" opacity=".7">35 times in 10¹¹</text></svg>

The exact hit. If the doubling lands exactly on the modulus (2u = m), pool and block run out at the same moment and the machine is left with an odd pool of 2m − 3 ones and an empty block. An odd pool is the only dangerous thing: the block doubles (0, 2, 6, 14, … pairs) and the pool pays 2, 6, 14, … until it cannot. If it comes down to exactly one 1, with no bracket to the left, the machine halts. Otherwise the leftovers are parked as a bracket (or an existing bracket is swallowed), the pool is even again, and the doubling map resumes.

So the machine halts exactly when the pool turns odd, without a bracket, at a modulus of the form m = 2k+1 − k (the pool is then 2k+2 − 2k − 3: 3, 9, 23, 53, 115, …). Such moduli get rarer and rarer, and the map passes each of them only briefly.

sections.eyebrow: How far it has been followed
sections.heading: 10¹¹ operations, 18 dangerous moments, no halt
html:
The map is exact arithmetic on three numbers, so it can be run far beyond what a step-by-step simulation reaches: 1011 operations are about 5·1010 visits of the right end, of the order of 1031 steps of the machine. In that time the pool turned odd 35 times, 18 times without a bracket, with pools

5, 13, 165, 989, 1853, 13309, 26333, 44669, 49909, 19855861, 169438117, 283866789, 1487681501, 1992437437, 3603147421, 10918121213, 46694013501, 51055443101.

None is a halting pool. The closest was 989: a pool of 1005 would have halted. All of them leave remainder 5 when divided by 8, which three halting pools in four do not; the fourth kind (53, 1005, 16357, …) is possible, and a tape like 1^12 0 (10)^19 does halt after five more visits. There is no parity argument left to find here: the outcome depends on where a chaotic doubling map lands.

The odds. The next halting moduli are near 237, 241, …; the map spends about two operations at each modulus, and each has about one chance in m of an exact hit. That makes a halt after this point about a 10−11 event. It is an estimate, not a proof: the machine most likely runs forever, and nobody can prove it.

explainer.title: A doubling map that halts only on an exact hit

family: doubling map with a growing modulus (odd-pool events)
summary: Its right-end map is proved in Lean (kernel: halts iff the map reaches T(none, 1, b)): a pool/pair-block pair that doubles u modulo a slowly growing m; when 2u = m the pool turns odd, and it halts iff that happens without a bracket at m = 2^(k+1) − k. No halt in 10^11 operations (5·10^10 visits); open.
